SEARCH
Package org.aeonbits.owner

Annotation Type Config.Sensitive

Enclosing interface:
Config
@Retention(RUNTIME) @Target({METHOD,TYPE}) @Documented public static @interface Config.Sensitive
Marks a property as sensitive, so that its value is replaced by MASK in the output meant to be read by a human: Accessible.list(java.io.PrintStream), Accessible.list(java.io.PrintWriter) and toString().

A password written in clear in a properties file is a value like any other to this library, and cfg.list(System.out) is a line people write while debugging and forget in the code. This annotation is how a property says that it should not end up in a log.

Only the human-readable output is masked, and for two distinct reasons that happen to point the same way. Accessible.store(java.io.OutputStream, String) and Accessible.storeToXML(java.io.OutputStream, String) write the configuration back: masking them would replace the value in the file the next time it is saved. The method itself, Accessible.getProperty(String), Accessible.fill(java.util.Map) and the JMX attributes hand the value to code that asked for it, which is the whole purpose of a configuration library. Masking is not encryption — see Config.EncryptedValue for that — it only keeps a value from being printed by accident.

The mask is per key, and a reference goes around it. With password masked and jdbc.url=...&password=${password} not, the listing shows the second line as it was written, ${password} included, and the secret does not appear. This is one of the reasons Accessible.list(java.io.PrintStream) does not expand the variables where Accessible.getProperty(String) does: an expanded listing would print the masked value in clear inside the line that refers to it.

When applied to an interface, all the properties declared in that interface are masked - the ones it declares, and no others. A sub-interface saying this does not mask the keys its parent declared, and a parent saying it does not reach what a sub-interface declares: an interface governs what it declares, which is the rule every annotation about the methods of an interface follows here. Write it where the methods are, or on the methods. See the documentation, Where an annotation counts.

On a method that reads a group — one returning a Map, which resolves to a prefix rather than to a single property — everything under that prefix is masked, since there is no property of that name to mask on its own. All of it goes, not only the entries whose name looks like a secret: the annotation says the group is sensitive, and guessing which parts of it really are would be a different feature. Where one method declares a group sensitive and another reads a key inside it and does not, the mask wins.

The keys to mask are worked out when the Config object is created, from the methods that take no parameters: a key that depends on the invocation arguments, or on a variable expanded at access time, is not known in advance and is left alone. A property that no method of the interface reads cannot be masked either, there being nothing to write the annotation on.

2.0.0
